top_choice_rationale: P001 (Calvo, Taylor, Woodford; B014) credits three separable, load-bearing contributions: Calvo's tractable time-dependent pricing friction, Taylor's staggered contracts and policy rule, and Woodford's welfare-based synthesis of interest rates, prices and optimal policy. Together they are the most original, broad and durable body of work on the shortlist. It has shaped both research practice and policy analysis for 25 to 40 years and has been revised and extended, not abandoned, after 2008, the zero lower bound and the 2021-23 inflation. None of the earlier macro prizes recognised this core. I weigh the real attribution cost: Galí, Christiano, Eichenbaum, Evans, Smets, Wouters and Gertler are excluded by the three-name cap. A citation limited to the three named components, which does not claim the estimated-DSGE tradition, reduces that cost without removing it. I rank P002 (Kiyotaki and Moore) second. It has the cleaner two-name attribution and a mechanism distinct from the 2022 prize, but a narrower footprint, and its original paper is theoretical, with identification coming mostly from later work. A defensible award is preferable to no award, so P000 is last. I count the ten explicit P001 supporters, which would clear the six-vote majority, only as a signal and give them no weight as merit.
recusal_note: None apparent from profile. My profile shows no co-authorship or institutional link to Calvo, Taylor, Woodford, Kiyotaki or Moore. My field is microeconomic theory and market design, which is adjacent to B006 but not to either ranked prize proposal. I am a Lund colleague of Kerstin Enflo and an SSE affiliate alongside committee members Dreber Almenberg, Friberg and Strömberg. These are ties to colleagues, not candidates. Disclosed, not adjudicated.
